I have previously written about the $\ell^2$-alexander torsion, [see here](../l2-alexander-torsion-thurston-norm/).
In fact, this was the topic of my masters thesis, in which I related it to the
thurston norm, [see here](../masterarbeit/).
This in is very closely related to the knot theory work I have been doing during
my masters degree in mathematics, for which I for example examined the
peripheral system of knots and created an 
[animation video for a talk I held about this topic](../knot-theory-peripheral-system/).

All this is closely related to the alexander polynomial, a tool used in knot
theory to distinguish between different knots (the running theme here being,
that we use algebra to tackle topological problems).

Another prominent example of an algebraic gadget used in knot theory is the
Jones polynomial. Together, the Jones and the Alexander polynomial are examples
of _[quantum invariants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_invariant)_.

---

:::{#def-quantum-invariants}
A **quantum invariant** $(\frak{g}, V, \epsilon)$ is given by

- a complex simple Lie algebra $\frak{g}$,
- a finite-dimensional representation $V$ of $\frak{g}$,
- $\epsilon \in \{0, 1\}$ specifies if we consider the _uncategorified_ ($\epsilon = 0$) or _categorified_ ($\epsilon = 1$) version of the invariant.

:::

Some of these terms will already be familiar from my post about Lie-groups:
</posts/lie-groups-and-algebras/#the-lie-algebra-of-rotations-so-3>.

There we defined a **Lie algebra** $(\frak{g}, [\cdot, \cdot])$ as a vector space $\frak{g}$ together with a 
bilinear map $[\cdot, \cdot] : \frak{g} \times \frak{g} \to \frak{g}$ 
called the **Lie bracket** satisfying:

- *Antisymmetry*: $[x, y] = -[y, x]$ for all $x, y \in \frak{g}$,
- *Jacobi identity*: $[x, [y, z]] + [y, [z, x]] + [z, [x, y]] = 0$ for all $x, y, z \in \frak{g}$.

Lie algebras can be found as the tangent space at the identity of a Lie group, 
as we have seen in the case of $\text{SO}(3)$. The Lie bracket 

By prepending "complex", we propagate that attribute down to the underlying 
vector space: $\frak{g} \in \texttt{Vect}_{\mathbb{C}}$.
